clue.text: Be really efficient as roundsman?

parts.note: the idiom for doing what is promised is read literally as the work of a delivery roundsman bringing parcels and milk to doors

explanation.surface: A question about what makes a delivery man truly good at the job.
explanation.walkthrough: A roundsman is a British tradesman with a regular delivery round, such as a milkman; the phrase for meeting expectations describes his job exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to fulfil a promise or perform as expected, which is what being really efficient amounts to.

clue.text: Workplace best for computer

parts.note: a desk is where an office worker does the job
top means best, as in top marks

explanation.surface: Someone recommends the ideal place to set up a PC.
explanation.definitionFit: A desktop is a personal computer sized to sit on a desk, as opposed to a laptop.

clue.text: Have fun up in the bar

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards, so backwards

parts.note: to revel is to have fun and make merry

explanation.surface: An invitation to enjoy yourself upstairs in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns REVEL round to give the answer; 'bar' looks like a pub but is a rigid rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A lever is a rigid rod pivoted to shift a load, so a kind of bar.

clue.text: Unusual relatives of many-sided ability

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters of the next word are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A remark about gifted but eccentric family members.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone versatile is able to turn to many different tasks, so has talents on many sides.

clue.text: Almost rely on leisure for escape

indicators.note: almost means the following word loses its final letter, stopping just short

parts.note: ease is rest or leisure, as in a life of ease

explanation.surface: Advice to depend on free time as a way of getting away from things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims the last letter from 'rely', leaving REL; 'on' simply joins it to EASE.
explanation.definitionFit: A release is a liberation or getting free, which is what an escape is.

clue.text: Listen to a number offer encouragement

parts.note: to hear is to listen to something
ten is one number among many

explanation.surface: A motivational coach asks people to listen to a numbered list of reassurances.
explanation.definitionFit: To hearten is to cheer up or give courage, which is offering encouragement.

clue.text: Admits US troops brought about victory in Europe

indicators.note: brought about here means placed around, so the soldiers surround the other piece

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers
VE stands for Victory in Europe, as in VE Day of 1945

explanation.surface: A historian concedes that American soldiers won the war in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought about' looks like 'caused', but here it means placed around; the surface's historical victory is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a point in argument is to concede or admit it, as in 'I give you that'.

clue.text: Some dragoons laugh, taking fierce attack

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Cavalrymen chuckle as they storm an enemy position.
explanation.definitionFit: An onslaught is a violent assault, a fierce attack.

clue.text: Guy's err badly doing these operations

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are put together badly, in a jumbled order

parts.note: the possessive's s counts as a letter here, giving the seven letters of the fodder

explanation.surface: Doctors at Guy's Hospital make mistakes while operating.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy's is a London teaching hospital, which makes the surface about medical blunders; here its apostrophe-s is a letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgery is the medical practice of operating on patients, so it covers those operations.

clue.text: After working out, reveals a number

indicators.note: working out suggests the letters are worked out into a new order

explanation.surface: A gym-goer discovers a figure after exercising, perhaps on the scales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working out' looks like exercise or calculation; it is the anagram signal on 'reveals'.
explanation.definitionFit: Several means more than two but not many, an indefinite count.

clue.text: Notice face protection for teacher

parts.note: an ad is a public notice or advertisement
a visor shields the face, as on a helmet

explanation.surface: A school sign telling staff to wear face shields.
explanation.definitionFit: An adviser guides and instructs, much as a tutor or mentor does.

clue.text: Scold marine found with Moslem chief under canvas

indicators.note: under canvas puts these pieces inside the tent, enclosed by it

parts.note: a tent is made of canvas, so living under canvas means camping
RM stands for Royal Marines
an aga is a Turkish or Muslim commander or chief

explanation.surface: A nagging woman, a soldier and a Turkish commander all camp out together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under canvas' is the British phrase for camping, so the soldier and the chief sit inside the canvas; 'found with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a harsh, quarrelsome woman, a shrew; a scold is the old word for the same.

clue.text: Plate of fish?

parts.note: reads as a dish of fish served at table, but means one of the thin protective flakes covering a fish's skin

explanation.definitionFit: Fish skin is covered in small thin bony plates, each one a protective flake.

clue.text: Without initiative, but I have to succeed first

indicators.note: first places the word for succeed ahead of the other piece

parts.note: to pass an exam is to succeed in it
I've is the short form of I have

explanation.surface: Someone lacking drive insists they must get through before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' tells you to put the success ahead of 'I have', reversing the order the clue gives them in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone passive accepts what happens and takes no action, lacking initiative.

clue.text: Expletive, seeing damage from use evident in weapon

indicators.note: evident in means one piece is to be seen inside the other

parts.note: a sword is a bladed weapon
wear is the damage caused by use, as in wear and tear

explanation.surface: A user curses at the wear and tear visible on a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: An expletive is an oath or obscene exclamation, a word one swears with.

clue.text: Inquisitive about Georgia's bunch of flowers

indicators.note: about means the first word goes around the second

parts.note: nosey means prying or inquisitive
GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: A nosy person is curious about a bouquet belonging to someone called Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small posy, a little bunch of sweet-smelling flowers.

clue.text: Single diamond thus ignited a great passion

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
lit means set alight, ignited
ire is anger, a great passion

explanation.surface: A lone gem sets off an intense love affair.
explanation.definitionFit: A solitaire is a gem, typically a diamond, set on its own in a ring.

clue.text: Noble lady is unrivalled, but without money

indicators.note: without means the money letter is taken away

parts.note: peerless means having no equal, unrivalled
L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra, a unit of money

explanation.surface: An aristocratic woman is beyond compare though she has no cash.
explanation.walkthrough: L for pounds sterling comes from Latin libra; 'is' and 'but' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeress is a woman holding a title in the peerage, a noblewoman.

clue.text: Hampton's weird ghost

indicators.note: weird signals the letters are put into a strange new order

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Hampton Court, the London palace, is said to have an eerie ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampton Court Palace is famous for ghost stories; the possessive s is not a letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A phantom is an apparition or spirit, another word for a spectre.

clue.text: Top commander to drink more — getting drunk

parts.note: to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls

indicators.note: getting drunk suggests the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: The boss urges the troops to keep drinking until they are tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting drunk' scrambles only the word 'more', which follows the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A supremo is the person in overall charge, a supreme leader or boss.

clue.text: Spread round permitted range of colours

indicators.note: round means the spread goes round the second piece

parts.note: pâté is a savoury paste spread on toast
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: A rule about where a spread may be put.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's palette is the board of paints, and by extension the range of colours used.

clue.text: Labourer gives vegetables to social worker

parts.note: peas are green vegetables
the ant is a social insect and a classic worker

explanation.surface: A farmhand hands vegetables to a council caseworker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' suggests a council caseworker, but it is the ant, an insect living in colonies. 'gives' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A peasant is a poor farm worker who labours on the land.

clue.text: Bore is shockingly rude in the end

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters go inside the other word

parts.note: end is taken as written

indicators.note: shockingly signals the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A tedious person is outrageously impolite at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shockingly' rearranges 'rude' and 'in' puts the result inside 'end'. 'Bore' looks like a noun but is the past tense of bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Bore is the past tense of bear, which means tolerated or put up with.

clue.text: Hanging in French town

definitions.meaning: a tapestry hung on a wall
a town in northern France, famous for its tapestries

explanation.definitionFit: The French town gave its name to the woven wall tapestries it made, behind one of which Polonius hides.

clue.text: Quiet, even now

definitions.meaning: calm and without sound or movement
up to this time, as in it is raining yet

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both calm and motionless, and up to the present moment.

clue.text: Worked as doctor, but not for real?

definitions.meaning: rehearsed beforehand, done in a trial run rather than the real thing

explanation.definitionFit: A doctor carries on a medical practice; rehearsing is doing something in practice rather than for real.

clue.text: Begin working paving stone round

parts.note: a sett is a square paving block of granite
the letter O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A workman starts laying a circular paving stone.
explanation.definitionFit: To set to is to start work energetically.

clue.text: Cheat — twice, almost

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: twice means two times

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of cheating more than once, or very nearly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' removes the final S from TWO TIMES.
explanation.definitionFit: To two-time is to deceive a partner by secretly seeing someone else.

clue.text: By way of peak, following a flyer

indicators.note: following puts the earlier pieces after the letter a

parts.note: via means by way of, travelling through
a tor is a rocky hill or peak, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Directions for travelling over a mountain after someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following a' means the route and the peak both come after the letter A. A tor is a rocky hilltop in southwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is a pilot, someone who flies aircraft.

clue.text: Compromise course not recommended for the pedestrian

definitions.meaning: literally the centre of the carriageway, an unsafe place for someone on foot

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a moderate political line and, literally, the dangerous centre of a carriageway.
